deck.title: Some Reactions of the Halide Ions

front_blocks.md: Why does the reducing power of halide ions increase going down Group 17?

back_blocks.md: Going down Group 17, the halide ions become **larger**. Their outermost electrons are further from the nucleus and experience more **shielding**. The electrons are held less tightly and are therefore more easily **lost (donated)**, increasing reducing power.

front_blocks.md: The addition of AgNO<sub>3</sub> to a solution containing I<sup>-</sup> ions gives a yellow precipitate.

back_blocks.md: Iodide ions form **AgI**, a **yellow** precipitate when silver nitrate solution is added. Chloride gives white (AgCl) and bromide gives cream (AgBr).

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

The addition of AgNO<sub>3</sub> to a solution containing I<sup>-</sup> ions gives a yellow precipitate.
cards.back_md:
**True.**

Iodide ions form **AgI**, a **yellow** precipitate when silver nitrate solution is added. Chloride gives white (AgCl) and bromide gives cream (AgBr).

front_blocks.md: The silver halide precipitate that dissolves in **..........**  ammonia is AgCl, while AgBr only dissolves in **..........**  ammonia.

back_blocks.md: The silver halide precipitate that dissolves in **dilute** ammonia is AgCl, while AgBr only dissolves in **concentrated** ammonia.

back_blocks.md: A **reducing agent** is a substance that donates electrons to another species, causing itself to be **oxidised**. In Group 17, halide ions are reducing agents, and their reducing power increases going down the group.

front_blocks.md: What observations are made when concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is added to NaBr?

back_blocks.md: First, **white fumes** of HBr are produced. Then concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> oxidises HBr, producing **reddish-brown** fumes of Br<sub>2</sub> (g) and **SO**<sub>**2**</sub> (g): 2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l).

cards.front_md: What observations are made when concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is added to NaBr?
cards.back_md: First, **white fumes** of HBr are produced. Then concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> oxidises HBr, producing **reddish-brown** fumes of Br<sub>2</sub> (g) and **SO**<sub>**2**</sub> (g): 2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l).

front_blocks.md: When concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> reacts with NaCl, the H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is reduced to SO<sub>2</sub>.

back_blocks.md: With NaCl, concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> only produces **HCl (g)** (white fumes). The sulfuric acid is **not** reduced because HCl is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce it. Only HBr and HI are strong enough to reduce H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

front_blocks.md: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of silver ions with iodide ions.

back_blocks.md: A **yellow precipitate** of silver iodide forms. Unlike AgCl and AgBr, AgI does not dissolve in either dilute or concentrated ammonia solution.

cards.front_md: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of silver ions with iodide ions.
cards.back_md:
Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgI (s)

A **yellow precipitate** of silver iodide forms. Unlike AgCl and AgBr, AgI does not dissolve in either dilute or concentrated ammonia solution.

front_blocks.md: Describe the test for halide ions using silver nitrate solution, and explain why nitric acid is added first.

back_blocks.md: **Nitric acid** is added to remove any carbonate or sulfate ions that could also precipitate with Ag<sup>+</sup>. Silver nitrate solution is then added. A **white** (Cl<sup>-</sup>), **cream** (Br<sup>-</sup>) or **yellow** (I<sup>-</sup>) precipitate of the silver halide confirms the halide present.
